title: Is sleep compression therapy non-inferior to sleep restriction therapy? A single-blind randomized controlled non-inferiority trial comparing sleep compression therapy to sleep restriction therapy as treatment for insomnia

sections.abstract:
Insomnia disorder, affecting 10% of the population, poses a significant public health concern and is a risk-factor for many health issues. Cognitive behavioral therapy is first-choice treatment, but the key component—sleep restriction therapy—presents with side effects and adherence challenges. Sleep compression therapy, suggested as a potentially gentler alternative, has never been directly compared to sleep restriction therapy.

Single-blind trial at the Internet Psychiatry Clinic in Stockholm, Sweden. Patients with insomnia disorder were randomized 1:1 to evaluate non-inferiority of sleep compression therapy to sleep restriction therapy in improving insomnia and to compare important clinical aspects. Primary outcome: self-reported Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), assessed pretreatment, weeks 1–5, and week 10. Non-inferiority analysis based on intent-to-treat analyses with multiple imputation and mixed effects models.

Adults with insomnia ( n = 234; mean age 44.3 [SD = 13.7] years, 173 [73.4%] female) received treatment as a 10-week highly structured, therapist-guided online program, to strengthen experimental integrity and treatment fidelity. Both treatments improved insomnia severity with large effects. Sleep compression therapy failed to show non-inferiority with a conservative limit of 1.6 ISI-points (95% CI: −0.01, 1.70), gave statistically significantly smaller improvements ( p = .006), and was associated with slower improvements despite better adherence and somewhat less side effects.

This direct comparison and well-controlled trial provides empirically based support for clinicians to prioritize sleep restriction therapy over sleep compression therapy, while the latter can be a valid alternative when sleep restriction therapy cannot be used.

CompRest—a Comparison Between Sleep Compression and Sleep Restriction for Treating Insomnia. URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02743338?term=NCT02743338&rank=1

NCT02743338 .

Keywords: insomnia, sleep restriction therapy, sleep compression therapy, sleep efficiency

sections.methods:
This study is a single-blind randomized (1:1) controlled non-inferiority trial comparing sleep compression therapy (COMP) to the reference treatment sleep restriction therapy (REST), including 234 participants between April 2016 and February 2019 and conducted at the Internet Psychiatry Clinic in Stockholm, Sweden. The overall CompRest study was preregistered at clinicaltrials.gov ( NCT02743338 ), and at the Regional Ethical Review Board in Stockholm, and received ethical approval before the study started (Dnr 2016/44-31/4). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Reports from assessments with polysomnography of a subgroup of participants have been published elsewhere [ 19 , 20 ].

The study welcomed adults in Sweden, recruited through the homepage of the Internet Psychiatry Clinic, Psychiatry Southwest, Region Stockholm. Participants were screened for eligibility through online questionnaires and therapist interview by telephone. Inclusion criteria were: 18 years or older, > 10 points on the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) [ 21 ], fulfilling diagnostic criteria for chronic insomnia according to DSM-5 [ 22 ], ability to read and write in Swedish, being able to answer questionnaires online and to have no practical hindrance to participate.

Exclusions were primarily limited to conditions that might make internet-delivered treatment or sleep restriction therapy unsuitable: sleep disorders requiring other treatment (untreated sleep apnea or narcolepsy); major depressive disorder; >30 p on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale Self-rated version [ 23 ]; ongoing self-harm or high risk for suicidal behavior; comorbid disorders contraindicative of sleep deprivation (e.g., bipolar disorder); ongoing alcohol or drug abuse; use of medications with sleep-related side effects; night-shift work; previous experience with sleep restriction therapy, sleep compression therapy, or similar methods; unwilling to keep sleep medication stable (or stop using) during treatment; not completing the pretreatment assessment on time. The use of antidepressants was allowed if they did not affect sleep, and the use of sleep medication was not an exclusion criterion.

Randomization and assignment to interventions were conducted by individuals not involved in the study, in cohorts ranging in size from 3 to 43 with a 1:1 allocation ratio, utilizing an online service ( www.random.org/lists/ ). Participants, who self-reported the primary outcome, were blinded to their assigned treatment. They were only briefly informed beforehand that the two treatments they would be randomized between differed in that one had a slightly faster pace than the other, and that both were expected to yield similar results after 10 weeks. No information was provided regarding whether the treatment they had received was the one with the faster pace or not.

After screening, eligible participants were invited to pretreatment assessments. They logged their sleep and daytime functioning in an online sleep diary for a minimum of 7 days, filled out pretreatment assessments online, and wore an actigraph during pretreatment assessment and treatment. Participants were then randomly assigned to start either COMP or REST.

During the treatment period, participants continued to log their sleep and daytime functioning in sleep diaries and to wear the actigraphs. The ISI was filled out weekly during the first 5 weeks, and then again at week 10. Both patients and therapists rated patient adherence to the assigned method nightly for the first 5 weeks of treatment and therapists registered the current sleep window and time in bed for each participant during the same period.

To ensure unbiased comparability and fidelity in the delivery of each treatment where all things should be equal except the sleep window-algorithm described below, both interventions were administrated via an online treatment platform. The reference treatment REST was delivered as per standard procedures [ 7 ]. Both treatments consisted of eight modules with written materials delivered over 10 weeks. The modules were identical except for the instructions for the sleep window-algorithm. The first 5 weeks were a more intense treatment phase with six modules and active therapist-support via written messages. In the following 5 weeks, patients continued working on their own with the allocated treatment. At week 10, therapists and patients communicated again to address any concerns or difficulties and plan for the future (detailed description in the TIDieR-checklist, Table S1 , Appendix , p. 4).

Sleep compression and sleep restriction were both introduced in Module 2, which was opened in the middle of week 1 if the patient worked according to plan, and in Module 3, i.e. week 2 in treatment, patients were expected to start using their initial individual sleep window. Sleep restriction or sleep compression continued throughout the course of the 10-week treatment and this was the only sleep-related treatment component. Weekly revisions were performed until an optimal balance between sleep efficiency and sleep duration was achieved. This was operationalized as no changes to the sleep window for several weeks with SE falling between 85% and 90%, and the patient not experiencing bothersome daytime sleepiness, or was satisfied with their sleep, which sometimes required a higher (or even a lower) sleep efficiency.

At the end of treatment, as part of relapse prevention, patients made plans for the future, which could include continued revisions of the sleep window according to the instructions.

The treatment was entirely focused on sleep restriction or sleep compression, excluding all other sleep-specific components of CBT-I (e.g., stimulus control, relaxation), but contained components to enhance problem solving and motivation (e.g. a decisional balance work sheet) and ability to engage in the active sleep component. Eligible therapists have licensed psychologists and clinical psychology students in their final (fifth) year, or in the first year of clinical training post-MSc. All therapists received training in and delivered both treatments according to therapist manuals. They were supervised by a licensed psychologist with expertise in CBT-I (AR, SJ or EF), who monitored treatment fidelity through supervision meetings, and by reviewing therapist messages and providing feedback when needed. Therapist messages consisted primarily of validation and encouragement to continue working with REST/COMP, problem solving, and support to carry out the treatment (e.g., how to calculate or adjust the sleep window).

The length of the initial sleep window was equal to the average total time in bed recorded in the sleep diary during a minimum of 10 nights, minus one-fifth of the average wake-time in bed recorded during the same period. In the following weeks, if average sleep efficiency (sleep time/time in bed) for the previous week was lower than 85%, the sleep window was shortened by one-fifth of the average time awake during the sleep window for the same period.

The length of the initial sleep window was equal to the average total sleep time recorded in the sleep diary during a minimum of 10 nights. Please note that no minimum (or maximum) length of the sleep window was stipulated, as we wanted to ensure that the two methods would result in different initial sleep windows also for individuals with short sleep durations. This means that a participant who reported a very short average total sleep time (e.g., 3 h), would start with a very short sleep window (e.g., 3 h). In the following weeks, if sleep efficiency was less than 85% the sleep window was shortened by 15 min.

If sleep efficiency was between 85 and 90%, the sleep window remained the same as the previous week. If sleep efficiency was 90% or higher, the sleep window was extended by going to bed 15 min earlier. The 90% limit was chosen from the original instructions for sleep restriction [ 6 ]. A regular rise-time was set to fit the patient’s daily life (e.g. work-schedule and preferences). The rise-time was to be kept constant during the course of treatment and any changes to the length of the sleep window were done through adjusting the bedtime. However, if the patient’s circumstances changed (e.g., the patient had a new work-schedule that required them to be at work earlier than anticipated), a new rise-time could be decided upon and was then to be kept constant. Patients were encouraged not to take naps, or if necessary, to take a nap at the same time each day, before 15:00 and for a duration of no more than 15 min. Nap time was not included in the sleep diary-based calculation of sleep efficiency and sleep window.

Background data included age, sex, education, economic situation, occupation, medication use, depression symptoms assessed with the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale Self-rated version [ 23 ], and alcohol use with the Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test [ 24 ]. The treatment credibility questionnaire (TSQ) [ 25 ] was used to gauge treatment expectations. The treatment platform logged number of messages sent from therapists to patients and therapist time logged in to the platform which were used to evaluate the therapists’ activity.

Insomnia severity was the primary outcome and was measured with the ISI, a patient-reported, seven-item scale ranging from 0 (no symptoms) to 28 (most severe insomnia) and commonly used in evaluations of the reference treatment. The ISI has adequate psychometric properties and is sensitive to change [ 21 ]. Assessments with the ISI were performed at pretreatment, weekly during weeks 1–5 and at week 10.

Difference between the groups was used to test non-inferiority between the two treatments at weeks 5 and 10.

At the outset of the study, we selected a non-inferiority margin of 4 points, based on previous studies. However, upon closer examination, this corresponds to a relatively large effect size (medium to large according to Cohen’s d), prompting us to reconsider its appropriateness. As the study progressed, it became increasingly evident that non-inferiority margins should be more conservative, and the field evolved in this direction. Recently, Kyle et al. [ 26 ] found that sleep restriction therapy compared to sleep hygiene gave a mean difference in the ISI of 3.88 points (95% CI: 3.10, 4.66). Using the initial 4-point limit as a non-inferiority margin would have meant to risk of concluding non-inferiority even if the effect of sleep compression therapy were similar to that of placebo. Instead, based on recommendations from Althunian et al. [ 27 ], we decided to derive the effect of sleep restriction therapy compared to control treatment from a meta-analysis on sleep restriction therapy [ 7 ], which was found to be within the 95% confidence interval of 3.2–5.3 ( M = 4.2 points). Since we wanted to ensure that sleep compression preserved a 50% fraction of this effect, using the fixed-margin method, the non-inferiority threshold was set to 50% of 3.2, the lower margin of the confidence interval, equaling 1.6 points on the ISI. In the light of COMP demanding similar amounts of time and resources, and that any advantages of COMP are still largely unproven, we argue that it is wise to choose a conservative limit when comparing COMP to REST in the present context. The revision of the non-inferiority limit was made after data collection was ended but before analyzing the data.

Side effects were assessed at weeks 2, 4, and 5 using the side effects-checklist developed by Kyle and colleagues [ 9 ], with ratings of the presence (0 [No]/1 [Yes]) and impact on daytime function (0 [not at all] to 4 [very much]) of 12 different symptoms associated with sleep restriction therapy, such as fatigue, excessive sleepiness, and trouble concentrating. A total score, ranging from 0 to 48 points, was calculated based on the presence and impact ratings for all symptoms. A score of 0 corresponded to either not experiencing the symptom or rating its impact as 0. The questionnaire was followed by an open-ended question about other side effects that participants might have experienced (“If any side-effects you have experienced are missing from the list above, please describe them here”). The answers were used to collect data on serious adverse events such as life-threatening events, hospitalization, persistent or significant disability or incapacity or any other event that may require medical intervention to prevent these outcomes. We did not conduct a structured assessment to verify whether the reported symptoms or events were directly related to the treatment.

Treatment satisfaction was assessed at weeks 5 and 10 in two ways: (1) with the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ-8) [ 28 ], eight items rated on a scale from 1 to 4 per item, maximum total score 32, with higher scores indicating a higher degree of treatment satisfaction, and (2) with the questions: “To what extent have you been able to utilize the treatment so far?” and “How much benefit have you had from the treatment so far?” rated from 1 (not at all) to 4 (to a very high extent/great benefit), and “How labor-intensive and extensive has the treatment been so far?” rated from 1 (very extensive) to 5 (not at all extensive), and “Has the treatment been worth the effort so far?” rated from 1 (no, absolutely not) via 3 (yes, but only barely) to 5 (yes, absolutely).

Treatment adherence was assessed in three ways: (1) Participants’ self-rating of adherence to the assigned treatment method as “According to method” or “Not according to method,” noted in the sleep diary; (2) Therapists’ ratings of participants’ adherence as “According to method” or “Not according to method”; (3) Deviation from the current sleep window, monitored from the establishment of the first sleep window to the conclusion of week 5, and calculated as minutes difference between the prescribed sleep window and the recorded time in bed in the sleep diaries. Details on the adherence measures can be found in the Appendix , p. 6.

Daytime dysfunction was measured with eight symptoms from the Daytime Insomnia Symptoms Scale [ 29 ], recorded in a daytime log. Each symptom was rated on a scale from 0 (not at all) to 5 (very much), positive symptoms were inverted such that lower scores indicated better functioning, and scores were summed to create a total score ranging from 0 to 40 points (lower = better).

Details on sleep diaries and actigraphs are in Appendix , p. 7. Total sleep time and sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, number of awakenings, and time in bed were derived from sleep diaries and actigraphy recordings, and the diary also included ratings of sleep pressure/sleepiness and sleep quality. Sleep parameters were used as both outcomes and indirect measures of adherence and fidelity by evaluating if they aligned with expected change patterns for each treatment.

Intent-to-treat analyses were applied throughout the study and data was used from all participants providing at least one outcome measure ( n = 234). The primary outcome measure was the ISI, and the primary analysis regarding non-inferiority at week 10 was used to calculate power.

The original power analysis was based on a non-inferiority margin of 4 points on the ISI, an expected standard deviation of 6 points, an alpha level of 5%, 90% power, and a 15% expected dropout rate. Considering the research questions for the second part of this study (not included in this report), which involved additional treatments and comparisons across four groups, we aimed for a target of at least 180 participants. However, as explained above, we decided on a more conservative non-inferiority limit of 1.6 points [ 30 ]. Updated power calculations based on this limit, an expected standard deviation on the ISI of 4.2 points [ 21 ] and 20% attrition, show that 215 participants provide 80% power to determine if the lower limit of a 95% confidence interval is above the limit, indicating non-inferiority. Power calculation was done using an online service ( https://www.sealedenvelope.com/power/continuous-noninferior , 2016). We therefore aimed to include at least 215 patients, with an upper limit of 250 if study resources allowed.

Multiple imputations and mixed effects models were computed, and the 95% confidence intervals (CI) for the estimated mean differences of ISI at weeks 5 and 10 were used to test non-inferiority. Non-inferiority results were visualized using base R, and non-inferiority at each time-point was concluded if the CI:s did not cross the predefined limit.

A secondary test for ISI tested if any group showed superiority regarding change in insomnia from pretreatment to week 10, by evaluating the time^2*group interaction in the mixed effects model for ISI.

To explore potential differences between the two conditions, chi-square tests (treatment satisfaction and adherence rated by participants and therapist), linear regression with the group as a covariate (side effects), or between-group t -tests (treatment credibility and adherence to the prescribed sleep window) were conducted.

Outcomes from sleep diaries, actigraphy and daytime logs were assessed using mixed-effect models with the same type of predictors as for ISI, but random slopes were not included due to convergence failure. The variance–covariance structure was set to unstructured. For the last day of treatment, 95% CI for the mean estimated values for REST and COMP and mean difference between the two groups were calculated.

To determine differences in change trajectories, both interaction tests (i.e. time*group and time^2*group) were examined.

For further details on statistical analyses, see Appendix , p. 8.
sections.results:
As shown in Figure 1 , a total of 234 participants were enrolled and randomized, with 117 allocated to REST and 117 to COMP. Only 7 participants (5.9%) in REST and 6 (5.1%) in COMP discontinued the intervention, all agreed to continue assessments and were included in the analyses. The sample primarily comprised women in their middle age experiencing sleep problems for more than 10 years, with an average ISI-score indicative of moderate severity ( Table 1 ).

There were no statistically significant differences in Treatment credibility, number of messages sent from therapists to patients, or therapist time logged in to the treatment platform (details in Appendix , p. 9).

Attrition rates varied between 4.6% (primary outcome) and 45.2% (actigraphy), details in Appendix Table S2 , p. 8.

For insomnia severity, as shown in Figure 2 , both treatments yielded gradual improvements across the treatment period, with large within-group effect sizes (Cohen’s d [95% CI]; pre to week 5: REST = 2.04 [1.72, 2.35], COMP = 1.54 [1.25, 1.83]; pre to week 10: REST = 2.37 [2.02, 2.69], COMP = 2.14 [1.81, 2.45]), and small differences and overlapping confidence intervals between the groups, but with a faster improvement and stable advantage for REST compared to COMP, and a statistically significantly larger overall improvement in REST ( p = .006; Appendix Tables S3 and S4 , p. 10).

Insomnia severity during treatment. Note: Observed and estimated means for insomnia severity from pretreatment to week 10. For observed means, 95% confidence intervals are marked with different colors depending on group.

At week 5, COMP showed an estimated average ISI-score of 1.51 (95% CI: 0.75, 2.27) points higher compared to REST. At week 10, this difference had decreased to 0.84 (95% CI: -0.04, 1.73). Figure 3 illustrates that the differences in ISI-scores between the groups did not fall within the non-inferiority margin at week 5, and at week 10 the results are inconclusive. The effect sizes of the difference between COMP and REST were almost medium at week 5 (Cohen’s d = 0.45) and small at week 10 (Cohen’s d = 0.22).

Non-inferiority analysis of insomnia severity. Note: The x-axis represents the estimated mean differences on the insomnia severity index between sleep restriction therapy and sleep compression therapy at weeks 5 and 10.

REST was associated with a somewhat larger burden of side effects and the difference was statistically significant at week 2, but not at week 4 or week 5, (see Table 2 , and Appendix Table S5 , p. 10 for details). The three most common side effects reported at all time points in both treatment groups were “Tired/fatigue” “Sleepiness,” and “Lack of motivation” ( Appendix Table S6 , p. 11 for details). Two participants in the REST group reported serious adverse events during the treatment period. One participant was involved in a minor car accident, and another participant reported experiencing blurred vision for which medical attention was sought. Both participants continued with the treatment and did not experience any other severe events during the remaining treatment period. No participant in COMP reported any serious adverse events.

Note: REST = sleep restriction therapy; COMP = sleep compression therapy.

Two out of three treatment adherence measures differed statistically significantly to COMP’s advantage: patient-rated proportion of nights according to the method ( p < .0001), and therapist-rated adherence to the sleep window ( p < .0001), but not therapist-rated proportion of nights according to the method ( p = .625; details in Appendix , p. 12 and Figure S1 , p. 12).

Treatment satisfaction as measured with the CSQ was high and very similar in both groups, with no statistically significant differences at week 5 ( p = .62) or week 10 ( p = .82; details Appendix Table S7 , p. 12). There were no differences in how much the two groups reported they had been able to utilize the treatment, how much they had benefited, how labor-intensive and extensive they found it, or if they found it to be worth the effort, at week 5 ( ps = .15 –.61) or week 10 ( ps = .55 –.90; details in Appendix Table S8 p. 13).

Daytime dysfunction improved faster in REST, but the groups did not differ statistically significantly ( p = .54; details in Appendix Table S9 , p. 13 and Figure S2 , p. 14).

REST had a statistically significantly faster decrease in sleep diary-derived total sleep time ( p < .0001) and a more rapid increase in sleep efficiency ( p < .0001; details in Appendix Table S10 , p. 15 and Figure S4 , p. 16). The corresponding actigraphy-derived sleep variables showed similar trajectories of change but no statistically significant differences ( Appendix Table S10 , p. 15 and Figure S3 , p. 14). Sleepiness and sleep quality (i.e. from sleep diary) also increased faster in REST ( p s = < .0001 and <.0004 respectively, details in Appendix Table S10 , p. 15).

In line with the instructions for the two treatments, time in bed (both from actigraphs [ Appendix Figure S3 , p. 15] and sleep diaries [ Appendix Figure S5 , p. 17]) decreased faster in REST, whereas the change in COMP was more gradual ( p s = .03 and <.0001 respectively; for details see Appendix Table S11 , p. 16). Sleep diary-derived sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset and a number of awakenings improved faster in REST compared to COMP (Appendix, Figure S4 and Table S11 , p. 16).

After 10 weeks, we could see a tendency of somewhat better results on sleep continuity (sleep diary) for REST, however, all differences were very small and had partly overlapping confidence intervals (Appendix, Table S12 , p. 18).
sections.discussion:
This study aimed to evaluate if sleep compression therapy is non-inferior to sleep restriction therapy in improving insomnia severity, and if it results in fewer side effects, better adherence, and less daytime dysfunction. It also evaluated whether trajectories of change differed between the treatments.

Both treatments were associated with large reductions in insomnia severity, but with a conservative non-inferiority limit of 1.6 points on the ISI, COMP failed to present as non-inferior to REST at both 5 and 10 weeks. The between-group effect was medium at week 5 and small at week 10 in favor of REST, which also showed a statistically significantly faster improvement rate and a larger overall reduction in insomnia severity. These are important findings, considering that sleep compression therapy has been used as an alternative to sleep restriction therapy for a long time [ 16–18 ], and is suggested as such in contemporary treatment manuals [ 31 ].

The choice of non-inferiority limit is crucial for determining the results in non-inferiority trials. In other non-inferiority trials for insomnia, the limit has varied from 1.67 to 4 points on the ISI [ 32 , 33 ]. Given that non-inferiority must be contextualized, such variation is not surprising. In this context, we are not willing to sacrifice too much in effectiveness for the potential benefits that COMP may offer. If we had chosen a broader non-inferiority limit, e.g. 4 points, COMP would have been deemed non-inferior to REST. Nevertheless, we maintain that the current limit is justified in this context, based on its theoretical and empirical foundations.

In a clinical context, the effect on insomnia symptoms is not the only aspect to consider. We therefore also investigated the potential advantages of sleep compression therapy and found that it was associated with less burden of side effects, a difference which was statistically significant at week 2. Interestingly, treatment satisfaction was not higher, and daytime function was not better in sleep compression. We did find that two out of three adherence measures showed better adherence in sleep compression therapy. This is a potentially important difference with clinical implications, which may be related to the findings of less side effects in sleep compression therapy. However, in the current study, drop-out from the treatments seems to not have been affected by less side effects, as it was very low in both groups. It also did not lead to better outcomes on a group level, but could still be relevant for clinical decisions on an individual level.

The initial reduction in total sleep time during sleep restriction therapy is expected to elevate sleep pressure, as indicated by increased subjective sleepiness at bedtime. This is assumed to induce favorable changes in sleep patterns, including increased sleep efficiency and improved sleep quality [ 34 ]. However, the reduced total sleep time is also why sleep restriction therapy is often not used in patients with psychiatric disorders, such as bipolar disorder. The results from sleep diaries show that sleep restriction therapy did induce a faster decrease in total sleep time compared to sleep compression therapy and a faster increase in sleep pressure, sleep efficiency, and subjective sleep quality. This is thus important to keep in mind when choosing therapy for a particular patient. At week 10, as expected, all these differences were very small and statistically non-significant, indicating that sleep compression therapy had “caught up” with sleep restriction therapy in these respects.

In summary, although sleep compression therapy has some advantages over sleep restriction therapy regarding tolerability, it comes with the disadvantages of failing to be non-inferior, having a smaller effect on the primary outcome, and a slower rate of improvement.

Our findings thus constitute empirical support for recommending sleep restriction therapy as the first-hand choice over sleep compression therapy on a group level. However, this does not imply that sleep compression therapy should never be used. The large reductions in insomnia severity, well in line with previous studies, is an important reminder that both treatments are clinically beneficial and should both be considered before pharmacological treatments. There may be valid reasons to opt for sleep compression instead of sleep restriction, for instance, if patients are unwilling to undergo sleep restriction therapy, or if sleep restriction is contra-indicated due to medical (e.g., bipolar disorder) or occupational (e.g., professional drivers) reasons. Also, there may be other benefits of sleep compression therapy that were not investigated in this study, and potential moderators of effects for the two treatments, which should be investigated in future research.

The randomized controlled design, the large number, and the blinding of participants are core strengths, accompanied by the range of subjective and objective measures of outcomes and sleep parameters, and night-by-night assessment for the whole treatment period. The level of standardization and fidelity to each treatment regime was very high with very little risk of contamination since both treatments were text-based and internet-delivered. The exclusion of all other standard therapeutic techniques in CBT for insomnia further reduces the risk for confounders.

There are also limitations to acknowledge. The complexity of deciding the non-inferiority limit necessitates cautious interpretation. Not measuring side effects weekly is a study design limitation, as is the high attrition rates for actigraphy. The fact that we assessed the occurrence of serious adverse events through an open-ended question rather than asking directly about serious incidents during treatment may have influenced how patients responded. Additionally, our decision not to include a lower limit for the sleep window may have increased side effects in the REST group compared to sleep restriction treatments that incorporate a minimum sleep window.

The sample for the current study was predominantly well-educated and had, on average, low levels of anxiety and depression. This may limit the generalizability of our findings, particularly in relation to more diverse or complex insomnia patient populations, such as those with significant psychiatric comorbidities or other health issues. As such, the observed inferiority of sleep compression therapy in this sample may not fully reflect its potential for broader, more clinically diverse groups. Future research should explore whether the advantages of sleep compression therapy become more pronounced in such populations and whether the treatment might offer unique benefits for individuals with more severe or complex insomnia profiles.

It should also explore the mechanisms of sleep restriction therapy and sleep compression therapy more closely, with a focus on the role of sleep deprivation in relation to treatment response and side effects. Future studies should also explore how varying sleep window-algorithm designs and time-in-bed reductions impact treatment outcomes and adherence in randomized trials, potentially using a factorial design.

sections.conclusion: This single-blind, randomized controlled non-inferiority trial shows that both sleep restriction therapy and sleep compression therapy delivered as single-component treatments are associated with large reductions in insomnia severity, but sleep compression therapy fails to show non-inferiority using a conservative non-inferiority margin. Moreover, sleep restriction therapy exhibits faster improvement in insomnia symptoms and faster change in several sleep parameters, such as sleep efficiency and sleep quality. In contrast, sleep compression therapy is associated with better adherence and somewhat less side effects early in treatment. The results suggest that sleep restriction therapy should be first-hand option, and that sleep compression therapy can be a valid alternative when sleep restriction therapy cannot be used.
